title: Names Ordered by Height
statement:
You get two arrays of the same length: names and heights. Person i is called names[i] and is heights[i] centimetres tall. All heights are different, but two people may share a name.

Return the names ordered from the tallest person to the shortest.

examples.why: 181 > 170 > 158. The names follow their heights, not the alphabet.
Two people are both called Sam. Each name stays tied to its own height, so a map from name to height would lose one of them.

hints: You need to sort one array but carry the other along with it.
Pair each name with its height, or sort the indexes 0..n−1 by height.
Sort the indexes by heights[i] descending, then map each index to names[i].

explain.intuition:
The order comes from heights, but the output is names. So sort something that remembers both: either pairs (height, name), or plain indexes compared by heights[i]. Sorting indexes is the general trick for "sort one array by another"; it is the same thing you do in a UI table when clicking a column header sorts the whole row.

Do not build a map from name to height. Names can repeat, and the second Sam would overwrite the first. Heights are unique, so a map from height to name works, but it still needs the sort.
steps: Sort it with the comparator heights[b] − heights[a] so taller comes first.
Return names[i] for each index in sorted order.
pitfalls: Keying a map by name. Duplicate names collapse and a person disappears.
Sorting ascending and forgetting to reverse.
In JavaScript, calling heights.sort() without a comparator, which sorts numbers as strings (100 before 9).

solutions.title: Pick the tallest remaining each time
solutions.idea: Selection: repeatedly find the tallest person not yet placed.

solutions.title: Sort indexes by height
solutions.idea: Sort 0..n−1 by height descending, then read the names in that order.

followups: Heights may now repeat. Keep people of equal height in their original order. Which sorts guarantee that?
Heights are whole centimetres between 50 and 250. Can you sort in O(n) time?
